dossier.public_summary: The dip depth changes by a factor of several from sector to sector and even within the same pipeline, and only a few sectors show the signal. A strong secondary eclipse about half the primary depth and a transit that is too long for a planet show the signal is not a planet on the target but a chance blend or variable contamination.

reasons.why: depth changes dramatically between sectors, not a steady planet depth. Many sectors have formally non-detections while others are very deep, requiring the signal to be produced by varying contamination/coding.
reasons.value: p_constant 6.889e-88, depth_change_pct 729.5, per_sector depths -204 to 1429 ppm

reasons.why: variation is not between QLP/SPOC calibrations but within the same source across sectors, inconsistent with a planet on the target. True sector-to-sector calibration differences would be steady within a source, not this scatter.
reasons.value: verdict changes_within_a_source, TESS-SPOC p_constant 2.5377297577517022e-82, per-sector depths -204, -190, -98,...1429 ppm

reasons.why: strong secondary eclipse at one-third phase, about half the depth of the primary. Hot giant transits can show tiny secondary signals; 148 ppm at SNR well above the noise is typical of a small-star eclipse and not a planet of radius 1.727 Rearth (undiluted_depth_ppm 357.5).
reasons.value: snr 8.118 at phase 0.3305 depth_ppm 148.4 depth_over_dip 0.4452, best_brightening_snr 6.003

reasons.why: transit is much longer than a central planet occultation for TIC radius 0.8376? Gaia radius 0.9594× smaller, and duration/rstar mismatch shows low density, favouring a stellar companion blend rather than a planetary transit.

independent classifier trained on followed-up TESS candidates rates this as unlike a planet, supporting the blend interpretation against a flat bottom (shape v_sigma -2.85) and stellar radius alone, which alone do not prove a planet.
